report.source_text: Examination of the feet revealed a distinct boundary between normal skin and affected crusted skin overlying osteolysis (“split” sign) on the third toe involving circumferentially the entire toe (Fig. 1). It was slightly painful and associated with serous discharge but no discharge of the bony spicules. Additionally, there was a shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. The sensation and peripheral pulses of the feet were normal.

clinician.trajectory_summary: The patient, a 5-year-old girl, presented with a transverse cutaneous 'split' on the plantar aspect of the right third toe with serous discharge and shortening of the distal phalanges of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. Physical examination confirmed the 'split' sign on the third toe and the shortening of multiple toes. X-rays of the right foot revealed significant phalangeal resorption (acro-osteolysis) in the second, third, fourth, and fifth toes. Extensive laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, parathyroid hormone, anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP test, C-reactive protein, fasting blood sugar, serum calcium, inorganic phosphate, albumin, and thyroid function tests, were all within normal ranges, effectively ruling out common systemic causes of acro-osteolysis and supporting the idiopathic nature of the condition.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Initial presentation included a transverse cutaneous 'split' on the plantar aspect of the right third toe with serous discharge and shortening of the distal phalanx of the 2nd, 4th, and 5th toes.

Physical examination confirmed a distinct boundary between normal skin and affected crusted skin overlying osteolysis ('split' sign) on the third toe, involving circumferentially the entire toe, and shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes.

X-rays of the right foot revealed complete resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the fifth toe, complete resorption of the terminal phalanx of the fourth toe, partial resorption of the terminal phalanx of the third toe, and partial resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the second toe, consistent with acro-osteolysis.

Laboratory investigations (CBC, renal/liver function, PTH, ANA, RF, anti-CCP, CRP, FBS, Ca, P, albumin, TFTs) were normal, ruling out infections, connective tissue, endocrine, and lipid storage diseases, and inflammatory/rheumatic disorders.
